messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: QA Engineer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 46

Mr. Vargas is a 75-year-old man who has been married to his wife, Elena, for forty-seven years. He presents as a gentle, soft-spoken man, given to long pauses before he answers a question, as if he is carefully checking his words for defects before releasing them into the world. He retired from his work as a quality assurance engineer five years ago, but the meticulous, process-oriented way he moves through the world has not retired with him.

The event that shattered his orderly world happened three years ago, when a catastrophic wildfire swept through the canyon community where he and Elena had lived for thirty years. He describes the day with a reporter’s precision: the exact time the sky turned the color of a bruised peach, the specific radio frequency that broadcast the mandatory evacuation order, the precise weight of the single suitcase Elena packed. They had forty minutes. He remembers checking the gas line to the stove three times, a compulsive, useless ritual. He remembers the roar, which he says was not like a train, as others describe, but like a living thing, a giant breathing in the dark.

In the present, Mr. Vargas cannot sit with his back to a door. He does not mention this; it is simply a fact of his existence, like gravity. At family dinners at his daughter’s house, he chooses the chair against the wall, his eyes scanning the room in a practiced, almost imperceptible sweep. His wife has stopped asking him why. The smell of woodsmoke from a neighbor’s fireplace sends him into a silent, internal retreat. He does not panic outwardly, but his hands still, his conversation stops, and he is gone, transported back to the ash-stung air of that afternoon.

His meticulous nature, once a professional asset, has become a cage. He now checks the locks on every door in their small apartment three times before bed. He checks the stove knobs four times. He has a spreadsheet on his old laptop that tracks the expiration dates of every item in their pantry, a digital fortress against the chaos of loss. He knows it is irrational, that a fire cannot touch them in this brick building in the city, but the logic provides no comfort. The feeling is older than logic.

Sleep is a battleground. He avoids it. He stays up late, reading old engineering manuals, the language of specifications and tolerances a familiar lullaby. When he does sleep, he dreams of the checklist. Not the fire, not the flames, but the list of things they might have forgotten. In the dream, he is running through the house, the air thick and hot, and the list is infinite, scrolling on and on: the photograph of his mother, his father’s watch, the box of baby teeth, Elena’s grandmother’s rosary. He wakes with a gasp, his heart hammering against his ribs, the name of the thing he forgot on the tip of his tongue. He never remembers what it is.

He is irritable, a quality he despises in himself. A dropped spoon on the kitchen tile makes him flinch. The sudden honk of a car horn sends a spike of adrenaline through his chest. He snapped at a young cashier at the grocery store last week for putting the eggs on top of the bread in his bag. He apologized immediately, his face burning with shame, but the damage was done. He saw the fear in the boy’s eyes, and he saw himself, a brittle old man held together by fraying threads.

He has not told his doctor about the nightmares. He has not told his priest about the way he sometimes feels a cold, sharp dread for no reason at all, a feeling that the world is about to be unmade again. He tells Elena that he is fine, just tired. He believes that if he can just control the environment, check all the boxes, verify all the data points, he can keep the world from burning down again. But the feeling of the fire is not in the world. It is inside him now, a quiet, steady heat that never quite goes out.
